body:
## Summary
The audit ledger has six insert sites and one retention update, and each builds the signed row by hand: stamp `at`, call `withAuditSignature`, stringify, create. Four of them were found unsigned one at a time and fixed one at a time; the comments say so. Add one door, `src/lib/db/audit-append.ts`, route every writer through it, and pin it with a guard that strips comments first and seeds a violation.

## Description
The registry's audit-logging `write-chokepoint` technique (law `one-validation-door`) says the ledger should expose exactly one insert operation, with every invariant inside it, so the writer list can be found by search. Today the invariant that matters most here, that the signed instant is the stored instant, is re-explained in a comment at every site (org-watch.ts:693, scans-persist.ts:793, scans-recommendations.ts:151 and :289), because getting it wrong makes a row verify as `tampered` forever. The door is `auditRowData(fields, at?)` (pure: one clock, sign, stringify), `auditRowsData(batch, sharedAt)` for the createMany case, `appendAudit(client, fields)` that accepts the prisma client or a transaction client so the in-transaction writers keep their atomicity, and `redactAuditRow` for the erasure update. `recordAudit` keeps its failure accounting (`noteAuditWriteFailure`) and its signature, so the 72 callers do not change. The guard follows the shape of `alert-door.contract.test.ts`.

## Flow
- Land audit-append.ts + audit-append.test.ts (cases 1-4, 8) red-first.
- Switch scans-audit.ts (3 sites), then org-watch.ts, scans-persist.ts, scans-recommendations.ts (2 sites), retention.ts (the redaction update), one commit each. The existing signing tests in those files stay green, which proves the bytes did not move.
- Land audit-writes.contract.test.ts (cases 5-7): red before the switch, green after.
- Update data-model.md section 'Audit-trail tamper-evidence': it still says the writers are `recordAudit` / `claimOrgAuditOnce`; it should name the door and the guard.

## Expected impact
A seventh writer cannot ship unsigned or mis-stamped, and the guard fails CI if it tries. The recorded write-path-sanitization deviation (scans-audit.ts:34) becomes a one-edit follow-up inside the door instead of a six-file campaign. Nothing is recorded less, no check is weakened, and the signed bytes are identical.

## Evaluation
Claim: every audit-ledger write goes through one door, and a guard keeps it that way
Before: 0 of 8 cases pass (the door does not exist; the guard finds 8 direct writes in 5 files)
After: 8 of 8
Method: gate - acceptance tests written red-first
Result: better
Gate: architecture

## Summary
The audit viewer verifies every row it shows, but it shows 25 at a time, and the tamper banner counts only rows already loaded. An examiner who sees no banner on page one has learned nothing about page forty. The server already walks the whole filtered trail for the CSV. Add one action, 'Verify all matching entries', that walks the same rows, returns counts by verdict and the tampered entries, and lets the reader switch the table to exactly those rows.

## Description
The registry's audit-logging `audit-querying` technique (law `count-carries-predicate`) asks that a count over a trail state the population it covers, and that evidence for an outside reviewer be checkable without paging by hand. Today the only whole-trail verdict is the per-row `integrity` column inside a CSV, which the reader has to open in a spreadsheet and filter. The new read-only `GET /api/audit/integrity` uses `requireOrgRead`, the same gate as `/api/audit`. It walks with `walkAuditLog`, the loop pulled out of `exportCsv`, so the sweep and the CSV cover the same rows by construction, under the same 10000-row cap. It returns `{scanned, ok, unsigned, tampered, noSecret, truncated, tamperedEntries<=50}`. A pure `auditIntegrityModel.ts` maps that to a strip state. `unsigned` stays neutral, as AuditLogCells.tsx already requires. 'Partial' names the cap and says the oldest rows were not checked, the same honesty as the CSV's -PARTIAL filename. The page-level banner is reworded to say 'on this page' and links to the sweep.

## Flow
- Reader applies filters (or none) and clicks 'Verify all matching entries'.
- The strip reads 'Checked 4,210 entries matching this filter: 4,020 verified, 187 unsigned, 3 tampered' with [Show the 3 tampered].
- Show tampered: the table holds only those rows (full Details, scan links). Back returns to the paged trail with its position kept.
- Changing the filters drops the stale summary.

## Expected impact
The question an examiner actually asks, 'is anything in this window tampered?', goes from N page loads plus a spreadsheet to one click. The signal the integrity work was built to give stops depending on how far someone scrolled. Nothing is loosened: the route is read-only, uses the same tenant gate, and its result is never shown as clean when it is partial or unverifiable.

## Evaluation
Claim: one action produces a verdict over the whole filtered trail and opens the tampered rows
Before: 0 of 8 cases pass (no walk module, no route, no model; the banner counts the loaded page)
After: 8 of 8
Method: gate - acceptance tests written red-first
Result: better
Gate: contract (new read-only GET route and response shape)

body:
## Summary
What a recommendation's status change MEANS is written inline in one HTTP route: a close feeds Shared Org Memory, a dismissal with a reason becomes a standing decision the next scan reads, and a reopen lifts that suppression. Every other path that moves a status skips all of it. That includes the rescan witness, which the claim module calls the only real close.

## Description
`PATCH /api/recommendations/:id` runs three consequence writers after `updateRecommendation` (route.ts:137-160), and grep shows they have no other caller. Meanwhile:
- the rescan carry-forward closes verified in_progress rows as `done` (scans-persist.ts:613-636), and Org Memory never hears about them;
- the loop's craft-rung close (lane-outcomes.ts:360) is an unguarded update with no consequences;
- any future writer (bulk triage, an Athena action) has to rediscover the three calls and their rules: run after commit, never throw, and a note is not a reason.
The result: Org Memory's 'recommendation-closed' events record human clicks only, while the trustworthy closes (measured by a rescan) never reach an agent.

The move applies the one-validation-door law behind remediation-roadmaps/sandbox-to-tracker-commit, plus scan-feed's own never-throw and idempotency contracts:
1. `src/lib/report/rec-transitions.ts`: a pure `planRecTransition({from, to, reason}) -> Effect[]`, the one place that says which transition earns which consequence.
2. `src/lib/db/rec-transition-effects.ts`: `applyRecTransitionEffects(effects, scope)` runs the existing writers (recordRecommendationClosedMemory, recordRecommendationDismissal, clearRecommendationDismissal) after commit and never throws.
3. Three callers: the PATCH route (same behaviour), the post-transaction block in scans-persist (resolved rows), and the craft close in lane-outcomes (now a CAS).

## Flow
- A writer commits a status change -> planRecTransition -> applyRecTransitionEffects (post-commit, best-effort)
- A rescan resolves a follow-up -> 'done' row -> close-memory effect -> episodic memory 'Recommendation closed on <repo>'
- PATCH dismiss with a reason -> standing-dismissal (unchanged); reopen -> reopen-decision (unchanged)

## Expected impact
Every verified close reaches Shared Org Memory, not only the ones a human clicked. The consequence rules live in one tested place, so the next writer gets them by calling it.

## Evaluation
Claim: status consequences live in one module and fire on every writer.
Before: 0 of 7 cases pass (the modules are absent; the persist and lane paths write no memory)
After: 7 of 7
Method: gate - acceptance tests written red-first
Result: better
Gate: architecture

## Summary
Today 'Commit N to tracker' writes blind. It doesn't show which of the tried items are already in progress, done, dismissed or untracked; it fires N separate PATCHes and reports only a count; and the rows it marks in progress have no holder on the Follow-ups ledger. Make the commit one previewed, per-item transition through the claim door the rest of the product already uses.

## Description
The sandbox is where a team decides its plan. The registry technique this surface was built from (remediation-roadmaps/sandbox-to-tracker-commit) asks for three things the bar lacks: show the extent before writing, keep per-item state so a partial failure names what failed, and make the commit one transition. The bar also routes around `claimFollowups`, the declared one claim path, so a sandbox-committed row reads 'in progress' with nobody holding it.

Build:
1. `sandboxCommitModel.ts` (pure): planSandboxCommit (start / skip with status / unmatched), summarizeSandboxPlan, commitOutcomeRows, plus the moved committableRecs, sandboxCommitNote and sandboxCommitSummary.
2. `SandboxCommitPreview.tsx`: before the commit, it lists the rows it will start and the rows it will skip, with the reason (in progress and the owner if any, done, dismissed, not tracked). After the commit, the same rows read tracked, held or failed.
3. Handoff route: optional `origin:'sandbox'` and `projectedDelta`. The org is resolved from the row (resolve-then-gate, as the per-id PATCH does), and the signed sandbox note is written. The default branch is untouched.
4. The commit bar makes one POST instead of the PATCH loop.

## Flow

Raise the public-org refusal from 31 per-route opt-ins to one door, `requireOrgAdmin(org, "admin"|"owner")` = `refusePublicOrgAdmin(org) ?? requireOrgRole(org, min)`, fold it into `requireOrgOwnerPost`, route the eight still-open owner/admin routes through it, and pin the rule with a comment-stripping source guard so the next owner route cannot ship open.

The ADR of 2026-10-07 decided nobody administers `public`, and chose a per-route helper over changing `requireOrgRole` (alternative 2 lost because hasOrgRole READ callers go through the same gate). It then recorded the price in its own Consequences: the rule is enforced only where someone remembered it, and no guard exists. That is the textbook 'rule re-broken at newly added call sites' (invariant-placement / placement-precedes-gate): the scan found 7 open routes, the follow-up found 14 more, and a grep today finds 8 more that neither pass reached, including both briefing-share routes behind the shared `requireOrgOwnerPost` preamble, the three practices writers, org/issue, registry dispatch and local/projects. - authz.ts: export requireOrgAdmin(org, min: 'admin'|'owner'); doc comment says it is THE door for owner/admin writes; requireOrgRole's comment points at it.

Let an owner paste a list of GitHub logins and emails, see before anything is created which are new, which are already members (and at what role), which already have a pending invite, and which are malformed, then create all the new ones in one confirm with per-row delivery outcomes.

## Description
Today onboarding a team is a loop: type one target, pick a role, submit, wait, repeat (MemberInvites.tsx:58-82). The leap is a preflight mode: the same pure classifier (src/lib/org/invite-batch.ts) runs in the browser for an instant preview and again on the server as the authority, so the client's plan and the server's outcome cannot drift. - Paste/type 'alice, bob, carol@x.io' -> preview strip: '2 new, 1 already a member (@bob, admin), 0 pending, 0 invalid' with each row listed.
- Confirm -> one POST {action:'batch', role, targets} -> per-target results in input order.
- Created rows join the pending list with copyable links; already-pending rows offer resend; already-member rows link to the roster row's role select.
- One target -> today's flow, unchanged.

Inviting N teammates goes from N submits to 1 paste + 1 confirm, and duplicate or redundant invites stop being creatable from the UI or the batch API. ## Summary
A GitHub-provenance token (the org's App installation mint or the operator's ambient GITHUB_TOKEN) is sent as a Bearer credential to gitlab.com whenever a `gitlab:` coordinate is scanned through the queue worker, the org import, or any caller that does not repeat the two scan routes' inline guard. Move the rule into one door, `src/lib/forge/scan-credential.ts`, that `scanRepository` itself calls, so a credential is bound to the forge it was issued for and no call site can forget it.

## Description
The rule exists and is correct, but it lives in two places it was fixed (`/api/scan`, `/api/scan/stream`) and is missing in three others: `scanRepository`'s own ambient fallback (scan.ts:227), the queue worker's `scanCredential` (scan-queue-worker.ts:232), and the import batch's single `scanOpts` (import/route.ts:237). Watched GitLab rows are rescanned by the worker on cadence, so the leak runs unattended, carrying a credential that can read the org's private GitHub repos to a third-party host. This is credential-vault / brokered-egress, *destination binding*: a credential is bound at admission to its home service, and the door refuses to apply it anywhere else. `ScanOptions` gains `tokenForge?: ForgeId`, default `github`: every token in the codebase today is a GitHub one, so an unlabelled token fails closed. The two scan routes label a caller-supplied body token with the coordinate's forge, which keeps a user's own GitLab PAT working. Wiring the org's stored GitLab credential (`getForgeCredential`, zero callers) is deliberately OUT of scope: this card only narrows.

## Flow
- add `bindScanToken({ forge, token, tokenForge, noAmbientToken, ambient })` -> `{ token, dropped? }` (pure)
- scan.ts:227 calls it with the routed `forge.id`; the ambient env token is offered only when `forge.id === 'github'`
- the two scan routes' `|| forgeId !== "github"` become the module's `ambientAllowedFor(forgeId)`, one rule
- scanCredential takes the job's forge from `splitForgeFullName(repo)`: non-GitHub -> `{ noAmbientToken: true }` without minting
- the import builds scanOpts per entry from `r.forge`
- a dropped token is logged once on the server (no value) so an operator can see the bind fire

## Expected impact
No GitHub credential can leave toward a non-GitHub host from any scan entry point, present or future, because the bind sits in `scanRepository` itself instead of at each caller. The rule goes from two inline copies plus three gaps to one tested module.

## Evaluation
Claim: a GitHub-provenance token never reaches a non-GitHub forge's fetch or enrichment.
Before: 0 of 7 non-guard cases pass (5 of them reproduce the leak through real call paths)
After: 8 of 8
Method: gate - acceptance tests written red-first
Result: better

## Summary
An org that connects a self-managed GitLab gets its host honoured for permalinks only. Every read (the snapshot, the MR/governance/CI enrichments, the cadence rescans) goes to gitlab.com at the same path: a 404 at best, and at worst a different public project's code scored into this org's row. The persist and watch layers then infer the forge from the url without the host and record the row as GitHub. Make the forge context a value that travels from the coordinate: one resolver, `resolveOrgForgeHost(orgSlug, forgeId)`, feeds `source(host)` and `enrich(host)`, and the adapter stamps `meta.forge`, which persist and watch read instead of re-guessing it from the url.

## Description
The ForgeHost seam was built (types.ts:67-72, `source(host)`, `enrich(host)`) and is wired at exactly one end: the import route's permalink. The scan path, which actually reads, never receives it, because `scanRepository` takes a string and re-parses it host-less. In connector-catalog / adapter-normalization terms, the adapter must own the facts it alone knows (which instance, which forge) and hand them to consumers in the model, rather than each consumer re-deriving them from a url. `forgeFromWebUrl` (registry.ts:115-133) calls itself a stopgap whose durable fix is `RepoMeta.forge`, and that field now exists unused. The resolver fails closed: a configured host that is not a public https host (isSafePublicHttpsUrl) refuses the scan with a fixed message and is never silently swapped for gitlab.com. Allowing an internal-network GitLab on a self-hosted deployment is a recorded residue, not part of this card, because the platform's server would otherwise fetch an admin-supplied internal URL. Local working copies keep persisting under their GitHub identity: `persistedForgeOf` maps `local` to `github` explicitly, the private-scan-scrub already relies on that, and local.ts:3's false comment is corrected. Sequencing: land card A first. Both cards edit scan.ts on adjacent lines (:226 source/host here, :227 token there).

## Flow
- org-forge-host.ts: resolveOrgForgeHost(orgSlug, forgeId) -> { host? } | { refused }; GitHub always returns {} (the GHES env vars stay the single source and github-parity stays reference-equal)
- scan.ts: when opts.orgSlug is set and the forge is gitlab, resolve the host, then parseForgeUrl(input, host) and forge.source(host); a refusal throws a fixed GitHubError
- scan-ingest.ts: IngestPhaseInput gains `host?`, and :133 calls enrich?.(input.host)
- gitlab/source.ts: meta gains `forge: 'gitlab'`
- registry.ts: persistedForgeOf(meta) = meta.forge === 'gitlab' ? 'gitlab' : forgeFromWebUrl(meta.url); local -> github is explicit
- scans-persist.ts:134 uses persistedForgeOf; org-watch RepoRef gains `forge?`, :182/:281 prefer it

## Expected impact
A self-managed GitLab org's import and cadence rescans read its own instance and land on one correctly-labelled row, where today they fail or score the wrong project. The identity is decided once, by the adapter, instead of being guessed from a url in three places.

## Evaluation
Claim: a GitLab coordinate in an org with a self-managed host is read from that host, refused when the host is unsafe, and persisted as forge 'gitlab'.

After: 8 of 8
Method: gate - acceptance tests written red-first
Result: better

## Summary
A tier is revoked by rank alone, so the revoke for a subscription that has already been REPLACED strips the tier its replacement is paying for. The grant already records its source (Subscription.stripeId); the revoke never reads it. Move the revocation decision into one pure module that scopes every downgrade to the granting subscription, and route all three downgrade sites through it.

## Description
Registry: software-engineering / plan-entitlements, technique `entitlement-lifecycle-revocation` ('The downgrade guard: remove only what this conferred': grants record their source; revocation is scoped to that source; one closed status set consumed by every reader). This repo's map already records the deviation (.ai/registry-map.json:8660). Concrete failures today: (1) an owner cancels Starter at period end, re-subscribes to Starter before it lapses; the old subscription's `subscription.revoked` floors the org to free while the new one is billing. (2) An owner moves Team -> Starter by buying a new subscription; the Team subscription's revoke floors them to free because pro ranks below team. (3) A full refund of an old renewal order does the same through a second copy of the guard, which also forgets to mark the Subscription row inactive. Nothing about what a plan grants changes: the same products grant the same tiers; the change only stops a revoke from removing a grant it did not make.

## Flow
- New `src/lib/billing/tierRevocationModel.ts` (pure): ENTITLING_SUB_STATUSES, planRank, subscriptionEntitlesTier (moved verbatim), and `decideTierRevocation({ cause, dyingSubId, dyingPlan, current: { plan, grantingSubId } }) -> { action: 'downgrade' | 'retain', reason }`. Order: grantingSubId set and != dyingSubId -> retain('replaced'); else rank guard (current outranks dying -> retain('override')); else downgrade.
- New `src/lib/billing/subscriptionRecord.ts`: getOrgSubscription(org) -> { stripeId, status } | null, and upsertOrgSubscription moved from the route.
- webhook route: downgradeSubscription and the full-refund branch both call one `applyTierRevocation(org, dyingSubId, plan, cause)` that reads plan + Subscription, asks the model, and on downgrade does setOrgPlan(free) + Subscription inactive. Refund passes order.subscriptionId (null for a one-time plan order -> rank fallback).
- billing.md: document source-scoped revocation, delete the stale :553 known gap.

## Expected impact
Closes a recorded registry deviation; removes a silent paid-customer outage on re-subscribe and on plan change; one status vocabulary instead of a route-private copy; the refund path stops leaving Subscription 'active' after a downgrade (which also skews freeToPaidConversion, src/lib/db/kpi-metrics.ts:208).

## Evaluation
Claim: every tier downgrade is scoped to the subscription that granted the tier, through one decision.
Before: 1 of 4 non-guard cases pass (none of the replaced-subscription cases; refund writes no Subscription row)
After: 7 of 7
Method: gate - acceptance tests written red-first (pure model tests + a route.revocation.test.ts sibling with the existing @/lib/db and @/lib/polar mock pattern)
Result: better
Gate: architecture (no change to what is paid for, prices, or which product grants which tier; only revocation scoping)

## Summary
The most anxious moment in the product - money left the account, nothing visible yet - is answered by a static sentence that says 'Payment received' whether or not anything was received, and never updates. Carry the Polar checkout id back, and let the banner follow that purchase through confirming -> paid -> landed (or stalled / failed / expired), painting the credits or tier when they arrive.

## Description
Polar substitutes {CHECKOUT_ID} into successUrl; orders.list filters by checkoutId; the webhook already writes an idempotent CreditLedger row keyed 'polar:<orderId>' and sets Organization.plan. Every fact the buyer needs exists; none reaches them. A new owner-gated, same-origin GET /api/billing/checkout/status reads the checkout (constrained to the org it was minted for), its order, and the local fulfilment, and returns one state from a pure model. The banner polls with backoff and stops at a terminal state. 'Stalled' (paid, not landed after ~10 min) shows the order id and says plainly that Polar is retrying delivery and what to quote if it does not land: today that buyer sees a banner promising 'within a minute' forever, and the usual reaction is to buy again. Registry: plan-entitlements `entitlement-lifecycle-revocation` law failure-not-empty-success, and feedback-and-style/async-ui-states (a pending state that names what it waits on and has an end). No change to what is sold, its price, what it grants, or who is charged: the route only reads.

## Flow
- checkout route: successUrl `...?credits=pending&checkout_id={CHECKOUT_ID}`.
- overviewBilling.resolveBillingReturn returns checkoutId and strips it from dismissHref; OverviewTab passes it to the notice.
- status route: polarEnabled / prefetch 204 / requireSameOrigin / refusePublicOrgAdmin / requireOrgRole(owner) -> polar.checkouts.get -> bound org must equal org else 404 -> if succeeded, orders.list({ checkoutId }) -> ledger lookup + planForProduct vs current plan -> deriveCheckoutReturn.
- checkoutReturnModel (pure): confirming | paid | landed | stalled | failed | expired | unverified, with the copy each state renders.
- useCheckoutReturn polls; on landed calls router.refresh() once so the credits chip and plan chip repaint.

## Expected impact
No false 'Payment received' on a bookmarked or failed checkout; buyers see their purchase land (and the amount) instead of re-buying; a stuck fulfilment produces an order id the operator can act on instead of a silent support ticket.

## Evaluation
Claim: the return banner reports the purchase's actual state and ends.
Before: 0 of 8 cases pass (the notice has two static states; no status route; no checkout id)
After: 8 of 8
Method: gate - acceptance tests written red-first (model unit tests, status route test with mocked Polar + db, hook/notice DOM test)
Result: better
Gate: contract (new read-only API route; checkout success URL shape changes)

## Summary
Declare the five scheduled jobs once (src/lib/cron-jobs.ts: path, schedule, required vs optional prerequisites, remedy per prerequisite, quiet-skip opt-in env) and derive from it: the vercel.json parity check, /api/health per-job readiness, and every cron route's precondition answer.

## Description
Today the cron surface is five hand-copies of one rule. purge and athena answer 503 on a missing DB because cron monitors only watch the status code; digest, rescan and probe answer a green 200 skip for the same misconfiguration, so a deploy that loses DATABASE_URL keeps three schedules silently green. /api/health reports readiness for rescan only, so the operator check docs/DEPLOY.md prescribes cannot see a dead purge or digest. The health route also carries its own copy of the constant-time secret compare. Health-checks three-state-outcomes and remediation-affordances apply: each job reports ready / degraded (optional prerequisite missing, partial run) / blocked (required prerequisite missing), each with the instruction that fixes it.

## Flow
- cron-jobs.ts: CRON_JOBS table + cronReadiness(probe) + cronPrecondition(name) -> NextResponse|null (503 on missing required prerequisite unless that job's opt-in env is set; purge keeps RETENTION_ALLOW_NO_DB, the rest use CRON_ALLOW_NO_DB).
- Parity test: table == vercel.json crons == src/app/api/cron/* directories, with a seeded mismatch proving the comparator bites.
- /api/health: internal callers get `crons` (per-job state/missing/remedy); `autoscan` kept as the rescan projection; the secret compare goes through cronSecretMatches.
- rescan/probe/digest/purge replace their inline checks with cronPrecondition(); athena is declared in the table and reported by health, but its call site is left untouched to avoid colliding with the in-flight athena card A (follow-up: one-line swap).

## Expected impact
A deploy missing a required prerequisite turns its cron monitors red on every affected job instead of 2 of 5. One GET to /api/health names every dead schedule and its fix. Adding a sixth cron without a table row fails the parity test.

body:
## Summary
Turn the error card from a report of state into a place to act: count retries so a failure that will not clear escalates instead of looping, give the user a one-click prefilled issue on the deployment's own tracker carrying the digest and a redacted route, forward caught boundary errors to Sentry once, and move the report permalink boundary onto the shared card so it gets the refresh fix it is missing.

## Description
The error screen shows a Reference digest but nothing can be done with it; a user who hits a deterministic failure clicks Try again, the card re-renders identically, and they cannot tell whether anything happened. Meanwhile the boundary only console.errors, so every client-side throw a segment boundary catches is invisible to Sentry - the crash-capture technique's inverted gradient: the careful code path (the one with a boundary) is the one that leaves telemetry. The report permalink boundary is a hand-rolled fork whose Try again is reset() alone, the exact dead button RouteError and global-error were fixed for. Error-handling user-facing-mapping: a suggestion that ignores the category (retry on a failure that is not transient) is worse than none, so after two failed retries the primary action changes to reporting.

## Flow
- routeErrorModel.ts (pure): errorKey, recordRetry(store) over an injected sessionStorage-like store (try/catch, degrades to 0), actionsFor(attempts), reportHref({digest, path, label}) with token-segment and query redaction, never the message or stack.
- RouteError.tsx: records retries, renders the escalated state ('Still failing after 2 tries - this is not transient' + Report this primary), captures to Sentry once per key.
- report/[owner]/[repo]/error.tsx: becomes a RouteError caller (fullScreen, homeLabel 'Scan another repo').

## Expected impact
Every boundary-caught client error reaches Sentry with its digest; a stuck user leaves with a filed, correlatable report instead of a loop; the report permalink retry actually refetches.

## Evaluation
Claim: the error screen escalates, reports and captures.
Before: 0 of 7 cases pass
After: 7 of 7
Method: gate - acceptance tests written red-first
Result: better
Gate: contract - adds an outbound link carrying the digest and a redacted path; no auth, billing or tenancy change.
